text: This paper puts a thought process\nthat stays small up against
a task whose output has to stay\nlarge — every pixel of it.
The encoder does the heavy lifting\nfirst, in the style SwinIR established.
Then the field is cut into windows, and\nnothing is pooled away on the way through.
The thought machine sits here in the\nmiddle, working on what the windows hold.
Only at the very end does the\ndecoder upsample, four times over.
That loop is a single tick, and it runs in
place rather than around\nthe whole pipeline.
Every tick reuses the same weights, so
thinking for longer costs\ntime and not memory.
Look at the bottom row of the\ncomparison figure — all three
approaches differ only in what\nthey hand the thought block.
The windows come first: the field is
partitioned, and each one\nis handled on its own.
The block in the middle is shared,\nthe same weights for every window.
And what comes out is still a dense field,\none query for every position in it.
Picture the feature map\nas a grid of tokens.
Attention runs inside\none window at a time.
The next window does the same, and\nat this stage the two never mix.
Count the tokens before a tick and\nafter it and you get the same number.
The encoder turns the low-resolution\nimage into a dense feature field.
The partition then cuts that field into\nwindows without throwing any of it away.
The window-wise version collapses each\nwindow down to a single summary token.
This one asks a question at every position\ninstead, and the token count survives it.
The partition is identical in both.
What differs is how much of it\nthe thought state ever sees.
These are five-benchmark averages\nat four times upscaling.
CATANet is the one to beat, at 29.48.
The method here comes\nin at 28.98 — ahead of
two CNN baselines, behind the transformer.
Only that last row was\ntrained for this paper.
Every other number is quoted.
The first tick is worth\nalmost a full decibel.
The fourth is worth under\na tenth, and training
stopped there, so nothing\npast it is demonstrated.
